title: People Skills
tagline: Listen well, handle conflict, negotiate, speak up and keep friends.
description: Practical, research-backed skills for dealing with people: real listening, easy conversations, feedback that helps, calm conflict, good apologies, fair negotiation, confident public speaking, and making and keeping friends. Every level includes scripts you can actually say.

units.title: Listening and Conversation
units.description: Listen so people feel heard, keep conversations flowing, and read people without guessing.

levels.title: Active Listening
levels.summary: Show people you heard them, and ask the questions that make them like talking to you.

steps.title: Most people listen to reply
steps.body:
In most conversations we are half-listening while planning what to say next. People can tell.

**Active listening** means your goal is to understand, and to show that you did. The core moves:
- **Attention:** phone away, face the person.
- **Reflect:** sum up what you heard in your own words. 'So the new manager keeps changing your shifts last minute?'
- **Ask open questions:** ones that can't be answered with yes or no. 'What happened next?'
- **Hold the advice** until you know they want it.
steps.tip: In your next real conversation, put your phone face down or in your pocket before the other person starts talking. It is a small signal people notice right away.

steps.title: Follow-up questions make people like you
steps.body:
Harvard researchers studied online chats between strangers and real speed dates. People who asked more questions were liked more by their partners. The strongest effect came from **follow-up questions**: ones that build on what the other person just said.

- Them: 'I just got back from my cousin's wedding.'
- Switching: 'Cool. I went to a wedding last year...'
- Follow-up: 'How was it? Was it a big one?'

Follow-ups prove you were listening.
steps.tip: Make it a game: in your next conversation, ask at least two questions that build on the last thing the other person said before you share your own story.

source.label: Huang et al. (2017), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, via Harvard Kennedy School

steps.prompt: Your friend says: 'I didn't make the varsity team.' Which reply is a good follow-up question?
options: 'I didn't make it my first year either. Anyway, did you see the game last night?'
'Oh no. How are you feeling about it?'
'You should just practice more.'
'Did you want to make it?'
steps.explain: It builds on what they said and invites them to share. Switching to yourself, jumping to advice, or a flat yes/no question all close the topic down.

steps.prompt: Match each reply to the listening move it uses.
steps.hint: A follow-up builds on a specific detail they just said. An open question can't be answered with yes or no.
pairs: 'So it sounds like you felt left out when they made plans without you.'
'Wait, the same coach who benched you last year?'
'Do you want ideas, or do you mostly need to vent right now?'
steps.explain: Reflecting shows you understood, open questions let them lead, follow-ups show you were tracking, and checking stops you from fixing when they just want to be heard.

steps.prompt: When someone tells you about a problem, the most helpful thing is usually to give them a solution right away.
steps.explain: Often people first want to feel understood. Jumping straight to solutions can feel dismissive. Listen and reflect first, then ask if they want ideas.

steps.prompt: Your younger brother comes home upset: 'Everyone at school is so fake.' You want to help. What do you say first?

options.text: 'That sounds rough. What happened?'
options.feedback: Short, warm, and it opens the door. You will learn what is actually going on before reacting.

options.text: 'You're being dramatic, not everyone is fake.'
options.feedback: Correcting how he feels shuts the conversation down.

options.text: 'Just ignore them. Find better friends.'
options.feedback: Advice before you know the problem. He may feel unheard.

options.text: 'Ugh, people at my school were the worst too. One time...'
options.feedback: Sharing can help later, but leading with your story moves the focus away from him.

steps.explain: Start with empathy and an open question. Advice can come later, if he wants it.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of listening to someone who is upset.
steps.hint: Attention comes before anything else, and advice only comes after you know they want it.
items: Put your phone away and give full attention
Ask an open question: 'What happened?'
Reflect what you heard in your own words
Ask whether they want ideas or just to vent
Offer help or ideas only if they want it
steps.explain: Attention, invitation, reflection, then check before advising. Each step tells them you care about understanding first.

steps.prompt: Which are signs of good listening? Select all that apply.
options: Asking about something they mentioned earlier
Checking your phone 'just quickly' while they talk
Summing up what they said before you respond
Turning every story into one about you
Letting short pauses happen without filling them
steps.explain: Remembering details, summarizing and allowing pauses all show attention. Phone checks and story-hijacking show the opposite.

steps.prompt: In your next three conversations this week, try asking at least two follow-up questions each. Who will you try it with?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Mom at dinner, coworker on break, friend on the phone...

levels.title: Starting and Keeping Conversations
levels.summary: Easy openers, keeping the flow, and remembering names.

steps.title: They probably like you more than you think
steps.body:
After a conversation with a stranger, people tend to **underestimate how much the other person liked them**. Researchers call this the **liking gap**. In studies, it showed up in labs, among college roommates, and at workshops.

Why it matters: if you think you came across badly, you are less likely to talk to that person again. Knowing about the gap can give you the nudge to follow up.
steps.tip: After meeting someone new and enjoying it, send a short follow-up within a day: 'Good talking today. Want to grab lunch next week?' They probably liked you more than you think.

steps.title: Openers that work
steps.body:
You don't need a clever line. Simple openers work because people are usually relieved someone spoke first.

- **Comment on the shared situation:** 'This line is wild. Is it always like this?'
- **Ask for a small opinion or help:** 'Have you tried anything here that's good?'
- **Give a genuine compliment, then ask:** 'Cool jacket. Where'd you find it?'

Then keep it going with **follow-up questions** and by **sharing a little about yourself** too, so it's not an interview.
steps.tip: Keep one go-to opener ready for places you wait in line or sit near strangers: comment on something you can both see, then ask a simple question about it.

steps.prompt: Match each opener to the type it is.
pairs: 'Did you understand the homework for question 4?'
'Your presentation was great. How did you find that data?'
'Hi, I'm Sam. I just started here this week.'
steps.explain: All four are low-pressure ways to start. The shared-situation and question openers are the easiest because they give the other person something to respond to.

steps.prompt: To be a good conversationalist, you need to be funny or have interesting stories.
steps.explain: Research on question-asking suggests that showing interest in the other person matters more. Asking good follow-up questions and listening makes people enjoy talking to you.

steps.title: Remembering names
steps.body:
Forgetting a name usually means you never really stored it. You were thinking about what to say next.

- **Say it back right away:** 'Nice to meet you, Priya.'
- **Ask about it if natural:** 'Is that spelled with an i or y?'
- **Link it to something:** a picture, someone else with that name, or something they told you.
- **Use it once** before you leave: 'Good talking, Priya.'
- **Write it down** later with a detail if it's someone you'll see again.
steps.tip: Right after you meet someone you will see again, add their name to your phone contacts with one detail, like 'Priya, from chem lab, loves hiking.'

steps.prompt: You met someone at a party 20 minutes ago and realize you have completely forgotten their name. They walk over to talk again. What do you do?

options.text: 'I'm so sorry, I'm terrible with names. Tell me yours again?' Then say it back and use it once.
options.feedback: Honest and easy. Almost everyone has done this. Asking early is much less awkward than avoiding their name for months.

options.text: Avoid using their name for the rest of the night and hope it comes up.
options.feedback: Possible, but you may never find out, and it gets more awkward the longer you wait.

options.text: Guess a name that seems close.
options.feedback: Getting it wrong is more awkward than asking.

options.text: Ask a friend later and never admit you forgot.
options.feedback: Not terrible, but the honest ask is simpler and only takes a second.

steps.explain: Ask early, apologize lightly, then use the name so it sticks.

steps.prompt: Which help keep a conversation going? Select all that apply.
options: Follow-up questions about what they just said
Sharing a related experience briefly, then asking them more
Answering questions with one word
Asking only yes/no questions
Picking up on a detail they mentioned ('You said you work at a bakery?')
steps.explain: Follow-ups, brief sharing and picking up details give the conversation somewhere to go. One-word answers and yes/no questions make it stall.

steps.prompt: A conversation hits an awkward pause. Which move is best?
options: Panic and leave
Go back to something they said earlier: 'Wait, you mentioned you're learning guitar. How's that going?'
Look at your phone until they leave
Start talking about yourself for five minutes straight
steps.explain: Pauses are normal. Picking up a thread from earlier is an easy restart and shows you were listening.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- People probably liked you more than you think. Follow up.
- Simple openers about the shared situation work fine.
- Keep it going with follow-up questions and some sharing of your own.
- Say a new name back right away, link it to something, and use it once.

**This week:** start one conversation with someone you don't know well (a classmate, coworker or neighbor) using a shared-situation opener and two follow-up questions.

levels.title: Empathy and Reading People
levels.summary: Body language myths, why lie detection fails, and what works better: asking.

steps.title: Empathy is a skill
steps.body:
**Empathy** means understanding what someone else feels and why, from their point of view. It is not the same as agreeing with them.

People often think they can read others accurately from faces and body language. Research suggests we are less accurate than we feel. In 25 experiments, trying to imagine someone's point of view did not make people better at reading them. Asking them did.

The most reliable empathy tool is simple: **ask, and listen to the answer**. 'You seem quiet today. Everything okay?'
steps.tip: When you catch yourself guessing why someone is upset, swap the guess for a question: 'You seem quiet today. Everything okay?' Then listen to the whole answer.

source.label: Eyal, Steffel and Epley (2018), Perspective mistaking, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: 93% of communication is nonverbal (body language and tone), so the words people use barely matter.
steps.hint: Think about whether you could understand a phone call or a text with no body language at all.
steps.explain: That figure comes from small 1960s experiments about single words spoken in a tone that didn't match them, used to judge feelings. The researcher himself said it doesn't apply to communication in general. Words matter a lot.

steps.title: You can't spot liars by their eyes
steps.body:
A big 2006 analysis of over 200 studies found people detect lies correctly about **54%** of the time, barely better than a coin flip.

Common beliefs like 'liars avoid eye contact' or 'liars fidget' are not reliable. Nervous honest people fidget too, and practiced liars can hold your gaze.

What this means for you: be careful about judging someone as dishonest from body language alone. Ask questions and check facts instead.
steps.tip: If you suspect someone is not telling the truth, skip reading their face. Ask a calm, specific question and check the facts you can check.

source.label: Bond and DePaulo (2006), Personality and Social Psychology Review

steps.prompt: In the 2006 analysis of lie detection studies, people judged truth versus lies correctly about what percent of the time?
steps.hint: Recall the lesson on spotting liars. Was its main message that people are good at this, or not?
options: About 54%, barely above chance
About 75%
About 90%, if they watched the eyes
About 30%, worse than chance
steps.explain: Around 54%, where guessing randomly would give 50%. Feeling confident about spotting lies does not make people more accurate.

steps.prompt: If someone avoids eye contact while answering a question, that is a reliable sign they are lying.
steps.explain: Gaze aversion is not a reliable lie cue. People look away when they are thinking, shy, anxious or from cultures where steady eye contact is less common.

steps.title: Better than guessing: name and check
steps.body:
Instead of guessing what someone feels, **name what you notice and check**:

- 'You went quiet when I mentioned the trip. Did I say something off?'
- 'You seem stressed. Rough week?'
- 'I can't tell if you're annoyed or just tired. Which is it?'

This gives them a chance to correct you, and it shows you're paying attention. Then listen without arguing with their answer.
steps.tip: Save this script for when someone's mood shifts: 'I noticed you went quiet. Did I say something off?' It works in person and by text.

steps.prompt: Your coworker has been short with you all shift. You're not sure why. What is the best approach?

options.text: At a calm moment: 'Hey, you seem a little off today. Is everything okay, or did I do something?'
options.feedback: Names what you noticed, gives them two easy options, and avoids assuming. You'll learn much more than by guessing.

options.text: Assume they're mad at you and be short back.
options.feedback: You might be wrong. Often people are stressed about something unrelated, and being short back escalates it.

options.text: Ask another coworker what their problem is.
options.feedback: This can turn into gossip and gets you secondhand guesses.

options.text: Ignore it completely.
options.feedback: Sometimes fine, but if it keeps happening, a gentle check-in clears things up faster.

steps.explain: Name what you notice, offer a check, and listen. It beats mind-reading.

steps.prompt: Which are good empathy moves? Select all that apply.
options: 'That sounds really frustrating.'
'You shouldn't feel that way.'
'What was the hardest part?'
'At least it's not as bad as what happened to me.'
'If I'm reading this right, you feel ignored?'
steps.explain: Naming the feeling, asking what was hardest, and checking your reading all show understanding. Telling people how to feel or comparing their pain to yours does not.

steps.prompt: This week, when you notice a mood in someone close to you, try 'name and check' instead of guessing. Who might you try it with, and what will you say?
steps.placeholder: e.g. My brother seems quiet after practice: 'You seem tired, rough practice?'

units.title: Feedback, Conflict and Apologies
units.description: Give feedback people can use, handle disagreements without blowing up, and apologize in a way that repairs things.

levels.title: Giving and Receiving Feedback
levels.summary: Use the Situation-Behavior-Impact method, and take criticism without getting defensive.

steps.title: Feedback can backfire
steps.body:
A major 1996 review that pooled 607 results from feedback studies found feedback improves performance on average, but in **over a third of cases it made performance worse**.

Feedback tended to backfire when it focused on the **person** ('you're careless') instead of the **task** ('this report had three wrong totals'). Personal criticism makes people defensive; specific task feedback gives them something to fix.
steps.tip: Before you give criticism, read your words back and swap any 'you are' label, like careless or lazy, for the specific thing that happened.

steps.title: Situation, Behavior, Impact
steps.body:
A simple way to keep feedback specific:

- **Situation:** when and where. 'In Tuesday's group meeting...'
- **Behavior:** what they did, as a camera would see it. '...you cut off Maya twice...'
- **Impact:** the effect. '...and she stopped sharing ideas.'

Then ask or suggest: 'Could you let people finish next time?'

It works for praise too: 'When you stayed late Friday to finish the display, we opened on time. Thank you.'
steps.tip: Write your next piece of feedback as three short lines first: when it happened, what they did, and the effect. Then say it out loud from those notes.

steps.prompt: Put this feedback in Situation-Behavior-Impact order.
steps.hint: Situation is when and where. Behavior is what a camera would see. Impact is the effect. The request comes last.
items: 'At practice yesterday,'
'you showed up 20 minutes late without texting,'
'so we couldn't start the drill and everyone waited.'
'Can you text me next time if you'll be late?'
steps.explain: When and where, what happened, what it caused, then a clear request.

steps.prompt: Which is the most useful feedback for a coworker?
options: 'You're kind of lazy.'
'Yesterday you left the dishes for the next shift, so we started 15 minutes behind. Can you finish them before you leave?'
'Everyone's been talking about how you don't pull your weight.'
'Try to be better.'
steps.explain: It names a specific situation, behavior and impact, plus a request. The others are labels, gossip or too vague to act on.

steps.title: Receiving feedback
steps.body:
Hearing criticism stings. A simple routine:

1. **Pause.** Don't argue right away.
2. **Say thanks:** 'Thanks for telling me.' (Even if you're not sure it's fair yet.)
3. **Ask for specifics:** 'Can you give me an example?'
4. **Decide later** what's useful. You don't have to accept everything.
5. **Follow up:** 'I tried what you said. Is it better?'

People who handle feedback well get more of it, and learn faster.
steps.tip: Memorize one reply for criticism so you do not argue on reflex: 'Thanks for telling me. Can you give me an example?' Then decide later what to keep.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: 'Your customer emails come across as a bit rude.' You feel your face get hot. What do you say?

options.text: 'Thanks for telling me. Could you show me one where it came across that way? I want to fix it.'
options.feedback: You stay calm, ask for a specific example, and show you're willing to improve. That builds trust fast.

options.text: 'I'm not rude, customers are just sensitive.'
options.feedback: Defending right away makes the manager less likely to give you feedback in the future, and you learn nothing.

options.text: 'Okay.' (and then say nothing and feel bad all day)
options.feedback: Not harmful, but without an example you don't know what to change.

options.text: 'Well, your emails are pretty blunt too.'
options.feedback: Turning it back on them escalates things and avoids the issue.

steps.explain: Pause, thank, ask for an example, then decide what to change. Arguing in the moment almost never helps.

steps.prompt: The 'compliment sandwich' (praise, criticism, praise) is the best-proven way to give feedback.
steps.hint: Ask yourself whether the lesson said anything about praise wrapped around criticism being backed by strong research.
steps.explain: It is popular but not strongly backed by research, and people often learn to brace for the 'but.' Specific, task-focused feedback, given respectfully, matters more. Honest praise is valuable on its own, not just as packaging.

steps.prompt: Which statements focus on behavior rather than the person? Select all that apply.
options: 'You didn't reply to my last three texts.'
'You're so selfish.'
'The report was missing the sales numbers.'
'You always ruin everything.'
'You interrupted me twice in that meeting.'
steps.explain: Behavior statements describe what happened. 'Selfish' and 'always ruin everything' are labels about the person, which trigger defensiveness.

steps.prompt: Write one piece of feedback (praise or a request) you could give someone this week using Situation-Behavior-Impact.
steps.placeholder: Situation: ... Behavior: ... Impact: ... Request or thanks: ...

levels.title: Handling Conflict
levels.summary: Start hard conversations softly, use I-statements, and de-escalate when things heat up.

steps.title: How it starts is how it ends
steps.body:
Relationship researcher John Gottman found that the first few minutes of a conflict conversation strongly predict how it ends. In one six-year study of newlywed couples, the first three minutes of a conflict talk even predicted which couples later divorced. Starting with criticism or sarcasm, which he called a **harsh startup**, usually leads to a fight.

A **soft startup** describes the problem without attacking:
- Harsh: 'You never clean up. You're such a slob.'
- Soft: 'I'm stressed about the kitchen. Can we figure out a cleaning plan?'
steps.tip: Before you bring up a problem with someone you live with, wait until you are both calm and fed, and open with how you feel about the problem, not what is wrong with them.

steps.title: I-statements
steps.body:
An **I-statement** describes your feeling and need instead of accusing:

**'I feel [feeling] when [specific event], because [why]. Could we [request]?'**

- 'I feel left out when plans get made in the group chat I'm not in. Could you add me?'
- 'I feel stressed when the car comes back with no gas, because I'm late for work. Could you fill it up?'

Watch out for fake I-statements: 'I feel like you're a jerk' is still an attack.
steps.tip: Before a hard conversation, fill in this line on paper: 'I feel ___ when ___, because ___. Could we ___?' Read it once out loud before you go.

steps.prompt: Which is a true I-statement?
options: 'I feel like you're being selfish.'
'I feel frustrated when you borrow my charger without asking, because then mine's dead when I need it. Could you ask first?'
'I think you should stop taking my stuff.'
'I feel that you always do this.'
steps.explain: It names a feeling, a specific behavior, why it matters, and a request. The others are accusations dressed up with 'I feel.'

steps.prompt: Build a good I-statement in the right order.
steps.hint: Follow the template: I feel, when, because, could we.
items: 'I feel annoyed'
'when music is loud after 11 on weeknights,'
'because I have to be up at 6 for work.'
'Could we agree on headphones after 11?'
steps.explain: Feeling, specific situation, reason, request. That order keeps it about the problem, not the person.

steps.title: Lowering the temperature
steps.body:
When someone is angry, logic doesn't land until they calm down.

- **Lower your voice** and slow down. People tend to match your tone.
- **Reflect their feeling:** 'You're really frustrated about this.'
- **Find something to agree with:** 'You're right that I should have called.'
- **Take a break if needed:** 'I want to sort this out. Can we take 20 minutes and come back?' Then actually come back.

If you ever feel physically unsafe, leave and get help.
steps.tip: Agree on a break phrase with family or roommates ahead of time, like 'Pause, 20 minutes,' so either person can stop a heated argument and come back to it.

steps.prompt: When you're angry, venting it out (yelling, hitting a pillow) is a healthy way to release it and calm down.
steps.hint: Think about whether practicing an angry action tends to make you calmer or more ready to be angry again.
steps.explain: Studies have found venting tends to keep anger going or increase it, compared with calming down or doing something distracting. Cool off first, then talk it through.

steps.prompt: Your roommate snaps: 'You NEVER take out the trash. I'm sick of doing everything around here!' It's not totally fair, but you have missed it a few times. What do you say?

options.text: 'You're right that I've missed it a few times, and that's annoying. Can we sit down and make a simple chore schedule so it's fair?'
options.feedback: You agree with the true part, acknowledge the feeling, and move to a fix. That lowers the heat fast.

options.text: 'Never? I took it out on Tuesday! You never do the dishes, by the way.'
options.feedback: Arguing over 'never' and counter-attacking turns it into a scorekeeping fight.

options.text: 'Whatever.' (walk away)
options.feedback: Walking away to cool down can be fine if you say you'll come back, but 'whatever' sounds like you don't care.

options.text: 'Calm down, it's just trash.'
options.feedback: Telling an upset person to calm down almost always makes them angrier.

steps.explain: Find the part that's true, acknowledge it, and move to a practical solution together.

steps.prompt: Which phrases help de-escalate a heated argument? Select all that apply.
options: 'Help me understand what upset you most.'
'You're overreacting.'
'I can see why that frustrated you.'
'Let's take 15 minutes and come back to this.'
'Here we go again.'
steps.explain: Asking, acknowledging and pausing all lower the heat. 'You're overreacting' and 'here we go again' dismiss the other person and pour fuel on it.

steps.prompt: Think of a small ongoing annoyance with someone (sibling, roommate, coworker). Write a soft-startup I-statement you could use this week.
steps.placeholder: I feel ... when ... because ... Could we ... ?

levels.title: Apologizing Well
levels.summary: What a good apology includes, and the fake apologies that make things worse.

steps.title: What makes an apology work
steps.body:
Researchers at Ohio State tested six common parts of apologies:
- expressing regret
- explaining what went wrong
- **acknowledging responsibility**
- saying you'll do better
- **offering to repair**
- asking for forgiveness

Apologies with more parts worked better. The most important by far was **acknowledging responsibility** ('It was my fault'). Next was **offering to fix it**. Asking for forgiveness mattered least.
steps.tip: When you mess up, say the words 'That was my fault' out loud, then offer one concrete fix, like 'I'll replace it Friday.'

source.label: Lewicki et al. (2016), via Ohio State News

steps.prompt: In the Ohio State research, which apology parts mattered most? Order from most to least important (of these three).
steps.hint: Look back at what the researchers said mattered most, what came next, and what mattered least.
items: Acknowledging responsibility
Offering to repair the damage
Asking for forgiveness
steps.explain: Owning it was the most important part, then offering to make it right. Asking for forgiveness added the least.

steps.title: Fake apologies
steps.body:
Some apologies make things worse because they dodge responsibility:

- **'I'm sorry if you were offended.'** Puts it on their reaction.
- **'I'm sorry, but you...'** The 'but' cancels the apology.
- **'Mistakes were made.'** Nobody did anything, apparently.
- **'I said sorry, what more do you want?'** Demands forgiveness.

A real apology: **'I'm sorry I [specific thing]. That was my fault. It [effect on you]. I'll [fix / change].'**
steps.tip: Before you send an apology text, search it for the words 'if' and 'but' and delete them along with whatever follows that shifts the blame.

steps.prompt: Match each apology to what's wrong with it, or right.
pairs: Blames their reaction, not your action
'Sorry I was late, but traffic was crazy and you're late all the time.'
'I'm sorry I forgot your birthday. That's on me. Can I take you to lunch this week?'
'I already apologized. Why are you still upset?'
steps.explain: A good apology is specific, owns the action, and offers repair. Fake apologies shift blame or rush the other person.

steps.prompt: Explaining why something happened always makes an apology weaker.
steps.hint: Watch the word 'always.' Is there a difference between explaining what went wrong and making excuses?
steps.explain: A brief explanation can help people understand, and it was one of the useful parts in the research. The problem is when the explanation becomes an excuse that replaces taking responsibility. Own it first, explain briefly second.

steps.prompt: You told a friend's secret to someone else and your friend found out. They're hurt. What do you say?

options.text: 'I'm really sorry I told Jake what you told me. That was my fault and I broke your trust. I won't share your private stuff again. Is there anything I can do to help fix it with Jake?'
options.feedback: Specific, owns it, names the impact on trust, commits to change and offers repair. Then give them time.

options.text: 'I'm sorry, but I didn't know it was such a big deal.'
options.feedback: The 'but' turns it into an excuse and suggests they're overreacting.

options.text: 'Sorry you feel that way.'
options.feedback: A classic non-apology. It doesn't admit doing anything.

options.text: 'I said I'm sorry. Can we just move on?'
options.feedback: Rushing forgiveness puts pressure on them. Trust takes time to rebuild.

steps.explain: Name what you did, own it, acknowledge the impact, commit to change, offer repair, and give them time.

steps.prompt: Which parts belong in a strong apology? Select all that apply.
options: The specific thing you did
'That was my fault'
A list of things they did wrong too
An offer to make it right
A demand that they forgive you now
steps.explain: Be specific, take responsibility and offer repair. Counter-accusations and demands undo the apology.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Own it clearly: 'That was my fault.'
- Be specific about what you did and how it affected them.
- Offer to repair, and follow through.
- Skip 'if' and 'but,' and don't demand forgiveness.

**This week:** if you owe someone an apology, even a small one, give it using this formula: 'I'm sorry I ___. That was my fault. I'll ___.'

units.title: Negotiate and Speak Up
units.description: Negotiate fairly using interests and your walk-away option, and give talks without freezing.

levels.title: Negotiation Basics
levels.summary: Interests vs positions, your BATNA, and why preparation wins.

steps.title: Positions vs interests
steps.body:
In the classic negotiation book *Getting to Yes*, Roger Fisher and William Ury describe a key idea: separate **positions** from **interests**.

- A **position** is what someone says they want: 'I need the car Saturday night.'
- An **interest** is *why* they want it: 'I need to get to work' or 'I promised to drive friends to a concert.'

Two positions may clash, while the interests underneath can often both be met. Ask **'What's important to you about that?'** to find them.
steps.tip: Next time you and someone want the same thing, ask: 'What's important to you about that?' before you argue for your side.

steps.prompt: You and your sister both want the family car Saturday. You want it to get to a 6 p.m. shift; she wants it to see friends at 8 p.m. What's the best approach?

options.text: 'What time do you actually need it? If you drop me at work at 5:45, you can have it for the night and I'll get a ride home.'
options.feedback: You looked past the positions ('I want the car') to the interests (getting to work, seeing friends) and found a plan that meets both.

options.text: 'I called it first, so it's mine.'
options.feedback: Arguing over positions. Even if you win, she's annoyed and the next fight is coming.

options.text: 'Fine, take it, I'll call out of work.'
options.feedback: Giving up your interest entirely when a solution for both exists.

options.text: Ask your parents to decide.
options.feedback: Sometimes needed, but you'll miss the easy solution you could find yourselves.

steps.explain: Ask about the 'why' behind each position. Often both sides can get what they actually need.

steps.title: Your BATNA
steps.body:
**BATNA** stands for **Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement**: what you'll do if this deal falls through.

- Selling your bike: your BATNA might be another buyer's $150 offer.
- Asking for a raise: your BATNA might be a job offer elsewhere, or staying at your current pay.

Your BATNA sets your **walk-away point**. Never accept a deal worse than your BATNA. And the better your BATNA, the more confident you can be. Improve it **before** you negotiate: get other quotes, apply to other jobs.
steps.tip: Before you sell anything, get at least one other offer or check recent sold prices online. Write that number down as your walk-away point.

steps.prompt: You're selling a used gaming console. One buyer has already offered $220 in cash. A second buyer offers $190 plus a $20 game you don't want and can't easily resell. Treating the game as worth $0 to you, how many dollars better is your BATNA (the first offer) than the second offer?
steps.hint: The game is worth nothing to you, so the second offer is really just its cash. Subtract that cash from the first buyer's cash.
steps.explain: $220 - $190 = $30. A thing you don't want is worth little to you, even if it has a sticker price. With a $220 alternative, you should not accept the second offer as is.

steps.prompt: In a negotiation, you should tell the other side your walk-away price right away to save time.
steps.explain: If you reveal your minimum, the other side will usually aim for exactly that. Know your walk-away point, but you don't have to announce it. Share your interests instead.

steps.title: Prepare in 10 minutes
steps.body:
Much of negotiating well happens before you start:

1. **Know your interests:** what do you really need?
2. **Guess their interests:** what do they need?
3. **Research the market:** what do similar things or jobs pay or cost?
4. **Know your BATNA** and walk-away point.
5. **Plan your first number:** first offers act as anchors, so make yours ambitious but justifiable with research.
6. **Think of trades:** things that are cheap for you but valuable to them.
steps.tip: Set a 10-minute timer before any negotiation and write three lines: what you need, what they probably need, and the lowest you will accept.

source.label: Galinsky and Mussweiler (2001), First offers as anchors, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Put these negotiation prep steps in order.
steps.hint: Start with your own needs, then gather facts, then set your limit, and only then plan your numbers and trades.
items: Figure out what you really need and why
Research the market price or pay
Identify your BATNA and walk-away point
Plan an ambitious but justifiable first offer
List trades that cost you little but help them
steps.explain: Start with your interests, ground yourself in market data, set your floor with your BATNA, then plan the offer and possible trades.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
steps.hint: Position is the 'what,' interest is the 'why.' Think of which term is your backup plan and which pulls the numbers toward it.
pairs: Your best option if no deal happens
A first number that pulls the discussion toward it
steps.explain: Knowing these four ideas covers most of what you need for everyday negotiations, from buying a car to splitting chores.

steps.prompt: Think of something you could negotiate in the next month (a price, a schedule, pay, chores). What is your interest, their likely interest, and your BATNA?
steps.placeholder: Negotiation: ... My interest: ... Their interest: ... My BATNA: ...

levels.title: Negotiation Scripts
levels.summary: What to actually say when asking for a raise, a better price, or a deadline change.

steps.title: Be warm and firm
steps.body:
Good negotiators are not aggressive. They are **friendly about the relationship** and **firm about the substance**.

Useful phrases:
- 'Based on what I've found, similar roles pay $X to $Y.'
- 'Is there any flexibility on the price?'
- 'What would it take to get to $X?'
- 'That doesn't quite work for me. Could we ___ instead?'

And a powerful one: **silence**. After you make an offer or hear one, pause for a few seconds. In MIT studies, negotiators who paused for 3 seconds or more reached deals that were better for **both** sides.
steps.tip: Practice one negotiation line out loud until it feels normal: 'Is there any flexibility on the price?' Then stay quiet and let them answer.

source.label: Curhan et al. (2022), Silence is golden, Journal of Applied Psychology (MIT open copy)

steps.prompt: You've worked at a store for a year and want a raise from $15 to $17 an hour. You've checked that similar local jobs pay $16.50 to $18. What do you say to your manager?

options.text: 'I've really liked working here this year. I've trained three new hires and covered extra shifts. Similar jobs nearby pay $16.50 to $18, so I'd like to ask for $17. Is that possible?'
options.feedback: Positive, specific about your value, backed by market data, and a clear ask. This gives your manager reasons to say yes and something to bring to their boss.

options.text: 'I need more money because my phone bill went up.'
options.feedback: Your personal costs are real, but they aren't a reason for the business. Focus on your value and market pay.

options.text: 'Give me $17 or I quit.'
options.feedback: An ultimatum is risky unless you truly have a better offer and are ready to leave.

options.text: 'Um, is there any chance of maybe a small raise someday?'
options.feedback: Too vague. Without a number or reasons, it's easy to say 'not right now.'

steps.explain: Lead with appreciation, show your value with specifics, use market data, and ask for a clear number.

steps.title: When they say no
steps.body:
A 'no' is often 'not like that.' Try:

- **Ask what's possible:** 'I understand. What would I need to do to get there?'
- **Get a timeline:** 'Could we revisit this in three months?'
- **Trade on other things:** schedule, hours, title, training, an extra day off.
- **Thank them** either way. You'll negotiate with them again.

And if your BATNA is better than what's on the table, it may be time to use it.
steps.tip: If a request gets a no, ask before you leave: 'What would I need to do to get there?' Put a reminder in your calendar to follow up.

steps.prompt: You're buying a used bike listed at $300. You've seen similar ones sell for $220 to $260. What's the best opening?
options: 'Would you take $100?'
'I've seen similar bikes go for around $230. Would you do $230 cash today?'
'Is $300 your best price?' and then accept whatever they say
'I'll pay $300.'
steps.explain: It anchors with a number backed by real research, and cash today is something sellers value. A lowball like $100 can insult the seller and end the talk; accepting the list price leaves money on the table.

steps.prompt: Making the first offer in a negotiation is always a mistake.
steps.hint: Watch the word 'always.' Think about what the lesson said about first offers acting as anchors.
steps.explain: Research on anchoring suggests a well-researched first offer can pull the final deal toward it. The risk is going first when you have no idea of the value. If you've done your homework, going first can help.

steps.prompt: Which are good things to trade on if they can't move on price? Select all that apply.
options: A better schedule
Extra training or a new skill
Threatening to post a bad review
A promise to revisit pay in 3 months, in writing
Agreeing to a lower price than your BATNA to be nice
steps.explain: Schedules, training and written timelines are real value. Threats damage the relationship, and accepting less than your BATNA leaves you worse off than walking away.

steps.prompt: You ask for a raise from $15.00 to $17.00 an hour. You work 20 hours a week. If you get it, how many more dollars will you earn per week before taxes?
steps.hint: First find how much more you earn each hour. Then multiply by the hours you work in a week.
steps.explain: $2 more per hour x 20 hours = $40 a week. Over 50 weeks, that's about $2,000 a year, which is why a 5-minute conversation is worth preparing for.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Be warm about the relationship and firm about the substance.
- Back your number with research, and ask clearly.
- Use silence after an offer.
- If they say no, ask what's possible, get a timeline, or trade on other things.

**This week:** look up the typical pay for your job (or a job you want) on two salary sites, or research the fair price of something you plan to buy.

levels.title: Public Speaking
levels.summary: Structure a talk, handle nerves with real evidence, and deliver it clearly.

steps.title: A simple structure
steps.body:
Most good short talks follow a simple shape:

1. **Hook:** a question, a surprising fact or a short story.
2. **Main point:** say what you want them to remember, in one sentence.
3. **Two or three supports:** examples, reasons or evidence.
4. **Close:** repeat the main point and say what you want them to do or remember.

Audiences remember far less than you think. Saying your main point at the start and end is not repetitive; it's helpful.
steps.tip: Before any talk, write your main point as one sentence on a sticky note. If you cannot fit it in one sentence, your talk is not ready yet.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a short talk in order.
steps.hint: Grab attention first, say your point, back it up, then say it again at the end.
items: Hook: a question, fact or quick story
State your main point in one sentence
Give two or three supporting examples
Repeat the main point and end with a clear takeaway
steps.explain: Hook, point, support, close. It's easy to remember, even when nervous.

steps.title: Nerves: say 'I'm excited'
steps.body:
Telling yourself to 'calm down' rarely works when your heart is pounding. In a 2014 study, people who said **'I am excited'** before a speech or a performance did better than those who said 'I am calm.'

The body signals of anxiety and excitement are similar: fast heart, energy. Calling it excitement helped people see the situation as a chance, not a threat.

Also helpful: slow breathing beforehand, and practicing out loud several times.
steps.tip: Right before you speak, take three slow breaths and say quietly, 'I am excited.' Do this in practice runs too so it feels normal.

source.label: Brooks (2014), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General

steps.title: They can't see it as much as you feel it
steps.body:
Speakers usually think their nervousness is obvious. In studies, audiences noticed much less than speakers expected. This is called the **illusion of transparency**.

In one experiment, simply telling speakers about this effect made them look more composed to observers, who also rated their speeches as better.

Your shaky voice feels huge to you. To the audience, you usually just look like a person giving a talk.
steps.tip: Record yourself giving a practice talk on your phone and watch it back. Most people find they look much calmer than they felt.

source.label: Savitsky and Gilovich (2003), Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Standing in a 'power pose' for two minutes before a talk is proven to boost testosterone and lower stress hormones.
steps.hint: Think about whether the hormone results of the original power pose study held up when other scientists tried to repeat it.
steps.explain: A famous 2010 study claimed hormone changes, but a larger 2015 replication did not find them, and one of the original authors later said she no longer believed the effects were real. Some people may feel a bit more confident, but the hormone claims did not hold up.

steps.prompt: Many speakers talk at about 140 words per minute. Roughly how many words should a script for a 5-minute talk be?
steps.hint: Words per minute times minutes gives total words.
steps.explain: 140 x 5 = 700 words. Most speakers write too much and then rush. If your draft is 1,200 words, cut it.

steps.prompt: You're halfway through a class presentation and your mind goes completely blank. What's the best move?

options.text: Pause, take a breath, glance at your note card, and say: 'Let me go back to my main point...' then continue.
options.feedback: A pause feels long to you but looks normal, even thoughtful, to the audience. Returning to your main point gets you back on track.

options.text: Say 'Sorry, I'm so bad at this, I'm freaking out' and stop.
options.feedback: Apologizing draws attention to the blank. Most of the audience wouldn't have noticed a short pause.

options.text: Fill the silence with 'um' until it comes back.
options.feedback: A silent pause looks more confident than a string of filler words.

options.text: Skip to the end and sit down.
options.feedback: You lose your best content. A short pause and a note card are usually enough.

steps.explain: Pause, breathe, check a note, and restart from your main point. Short silences are invisible to most audiences.

steps.prompt: Which preparation habits help most with speaking? Select all that apply.
options: Practicing out loud several times, ideally to a friend
Memorizing every word so you can't forget
Using note cards with key points only
Recording yourself once and watching it
Reading your slides word for word
steps.explain: Out-loud practice, key-point cards and a quick recording review build confidence and catch problems. Word-for-word memorizing can make you freeze if you lose one line, and reading slides loses your audience.

steps.prompt: Pick a talk, presentation or toast coming up (or make one up: 2 minutes on a topic you love). Write your hook, main point and close, then practice it out loud twice this week.

units.title: Friendships and Boundaries
units.description: Make friends as a teen or young adult, keep them over time, and say no without wrecking relationships.

levels.title: Making Friends
levels.summary: Friendship takes time together. Here is how much, and how to get it.

steps.title: Friendship runs on hours
steps.body:
A 2018 study at the University of Kansas asked adults who had recently moved, and new college students, about the people they had met. It estimated it takes about:
- **50 hours** together to go from acquaintance to casual friend
- **90 hours** to become a friend
- **200+ hours** to become a close friend

Time spent hanging out (joking, talking, doing things together) counted much more than time spent just working side by side.
steps.tip: Look at your week and pick one person you want to know better. Plan one extra hour together, like walking to class or getting food after practice.

source.label: Hall (2018), via University of Kansas News

steps.prompt: Using the study's estimate of about 50 hours to become casual friends: if you spend about 5 hours a week with someone (a club, a team, hanging out), how many weeks would it take?
steps.hint: Divide the total hours needed by the hours you spend together each week.
steps.explain: 50 / 5 = 10 weeks. That's why friendships form easily in school and on teams, and why adults need to create regular time together on purpose.

steps.title: Repeated, easy contact
steps.body:
Friendships grow fastest when you see the same people **regularly without having to plan it**: a class, a team, a job, a weekly game night, a club, a gym class, a volunteer shift.

If you're in a new place (a new school, job or city), the most reliable move is to **join one recurring thing** and keep showing up. Then take a small step: suggest getting food after, or invite one person to something low-key.
steps.tip: If you are new somewhere, sign up this week for one thing that meets at the same time every week, and commit to going at least four times.

steps.prompt: If you and someone don't click in the first conversation, you probably won't become friends.
steps.explain: Most friendships build over many hours of repeated contact. Plus, the liking gap means the other person probably liked you more than you thought. Keep showing up.

steps.prompt: You've been in the same weekly climbing class as Alex for a month and you get along. You want to become actual friends. What do you say?

options.text: 'Hey, a few of us are grabbing tacos after class Thursday. Want to come?' (and actually plan it)
options.feedback: Low-pressure, specific, and connected to something you already share. Even if Alex can't come, it signals you'd like to hang out.

options.text: Wait for Alex to invite you first.
options.feedback: They might be waiting for you too. Someone has to go first.

options.text: 'We should hang out sometime!' (with no plan)
options.feedback: Friendly, but vague invites rarely turn into plans. Name a time and place.

options.text: Send Alex a long message about how you want to be close friends.
options.feedback: Probably too much too soon. Small, easy invitations build friendship more naturally.

steps.explain: Make a specific, easy invitation tied to what you already share. Being the one who initiates is a superpower.

steps.prompt: Which are good ways to make friends in a new place? Select all that apply.
options: Join a weekly club, team or class and keep going
Wait for people to come to you
Invite one person to something specific and low-key
Volunteer for the same shift every week
Quit a group after one meeting if you didn't make a friend
steps.explain: Recurring activities and specific invitations add up the hours friendship needs. Waiting and quitting early cut those hours off.

steps.prompt: Match each friendship level to roughly how many hours together the 2018 study estimated.
steps.hint: The hours go up with each level, and a close friend takes far more time than the other two.
steps.explain: These are rough averages from one study, not exact rules, but they show that friendship takes real time, especially time spent hanging out.

steps.prompt: What is one recurring activity you're in (or could join) where you could build friendships? Who is one person you could invite to something specific this week?

levels.title: Keeping Friendships
levels.summary: Reach out, show up, and handle drifting apart.

steps.title: Friendships need upkeep
steps.body:
Friendships fade when contact stops, especially after moving, changing schools or starting a job. That's normal, but you can slow it down.

Studies suggest people **underestimate how much others appreciate** a quick, unexpected check-in, like a text saying 'Saw this and thought of you.' The other person usually values it more than you'd guess.

Small, regular contact beats rare big efforts.
steps.tip: Set a weekly phone reminder called 'Reach out' and use it to send one friend a quick message, like a photo or 'Saw this and thought of you.'

source.label: Liu et al. (2023), The surprise of reaching out, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Which are easy ways to keep a friendship going? Select all that apply.
options: Sending a meme or photo that reminds you of them
Waiting until you have something big to say
Remembering their big event and asking how it went
Setting a regular call or game night
Only reaching out when you need a favor
steps.explain: Small check-ins, remembering what matters to them, and a regular ritual keep friendships alive. Waiting for big news or only calling for favors lets them fade.

steps.title: Being a good friend
steps.body:
What people value most in friends is pretty consistent:

- **Showing up:** helping them move, coming to their game or show.
- **Reliability:** doing what you said you'd do.
- **Keeping confidences:** not spreading what they tell you.
- **Being happy for them:** reacting with real enthusiasm to good news. 'That's amazing! Tell me everything.'
- **Honesty with kindness:** telling them hard things gently when it matters.
steps.tip: Put your friends' birthdays and big events, like games or recitals, in your calendar with a reminder a few days before.

source.label: Gable et al. (2004), What do you do when things go right?, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Your best friend from high school moved for college and you haven't talked in two months. You feel awkward reaching out. What do you do?

options.text: Text: 'Hey! I was just thinking about that time we got lost on the hiking trail. How's college going? Want to call this weekend?'
options.feedback: Warm, references a shared memory, asks about them, and suggests a specific next step. Most people are happy to get this.

options.text: Wait for them to text first since they're the one who moved.
options.feedback: They may be feeling the same awkwardness. Someone has to go first, and it can be you.

options.text: 'Guess you forgot about me, huh?'
options.feedback: Guilt-tripping makes reaching back feel bad. Lead with warmth.

options.text: Decide the friendship is over.
options.feedback: Two months is not long. Many friendships pick right back up with one message.

steps.explain: Reach out warmly, mention a shared memory, and suggest a specific call or plan.

steps.prompt: Reacting enthusiastically when a friend shares good news is an important part of a strong relationship.
steps.explain: Researchers studying couples and friends have found that how people respond to good news matters. An engaged, enthusiastic reply ('That's amazing, how did it happen?') strengthens relationships more than a flat 'cool' or changing the subject.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: 'I got the internship!' Which reply builds the friendship most?
options: 'Cool.'
'Nice, I'm still waiting to hear back from mine.'
'No way, that's huge! How did you find out? When do you start?'
'Are you sure you can handle that with your schedule?'
steps.explain: Enthusiastic and curious. The others are flat, turn it toward you, or poke holes in their good news.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Small, regular check-ins keep friendships alive. People appreciate them more than you'd guess.
- Show up, be reliable, keep confidences.
- Celebrate good news with real enthusiasm.
- If you've drifted, a warm message with a shared memory and a specific plan usually works.

**This week:** text one friend you haven't talked to in a while with a shared memory and a specific invite to call or meet.

levels.title: Saying No and Setting Boundaries
levels.summary: Turn down requests and protect your time without guilt or drama.

steps.title: A boundary is about what you will do
steps.body:
A **boundary** is a limit on what you will accept or do. It's not a rule for other people; it's a statement about **your** actions.

- Not a boundary: 'You can't call me after 10.'
- A boundary: 'I don't answer calls after 10 on school nights. I'll call you back in the morning.'

You can't control what others do. You can control how you respond, and say it clearly and kindly.
steps.tip: Turn on your phone's Do Not Disturb schedule for the hours you want protected, and allow calls from family so emergencies still reach you.

steps.title: How to say no
steps.body:
A clear no is kinder than a vague maybe that turns into a late cancel.

- **Short and warm:** 'Thanks for asking, but I can't this time.'
- **No long excuses needed.** The more reasons you give, the more someone can argue with them.
- **Offer an alternative if you want to:** 'I can't do Saturday, but I could help Sunday morning.'
- **Broken record:** if pushed, repeat calmly: 'I get it, but I still can't.'

For work: 'I can do that, but then X will be late. Which should I prioritize?'
steps.tip: Keep one ready no: 'Thanks for asking, but I can't this time.' Say it without adding a list of reasons, then change the subject.

steps.prompt: A coworker asks you to cover their Saturday shift for the third time this month. You have plans and want to say no. What do you say?

options.text: 'I can't this Saturday, I've got plans. Hope you find someone!'
options.feedback: Clear, friendly, and short. You don't owe a long explanation.

options.text: 'Ugh, maybe? Let me see.' (then text no on Friday night)
options.feedback: A vague maybe followed by a late no is harder on them than a clear no now.

options.text: 'You always do this. Find someone else.'
options.feedback: You can say no without attacking. This damages a work relationship.

options.text: Say yes and cancel your plans, again.
options.feedback: Occasionally helping is kind, but repeatedly giving up your plans builds resentment.

steps.explain: A short, warm, clear no is best. If you want to help sometimes, offer a specific alternative.

steps.prompt: Match each situation to a good boundary script.
pairs: A friend keeps borrowing money and not paying it back
'I'm not lending money anymore, but I'm happy to help in other ways.'
Someone pressures you to drink at a party
'No thanks, I'm good.' (and repeat if needed)
Your boss texts you on your day off about non-urgent work
'I'll take care of that first thing tomorrow.'
A relative asks invasive questions about your weight
'I'd rather not talk about that. How's your garden doing?'
steps.explain: Good boundary scripts are short, calm and about what you'll do. Changing the subject is a valid way to hold a boundary.

steps.prompt: When you say no, you should always give a detailed reason so the other person doesn't feel rejected.
steps.explain: A brief reason can be kind, but long justifications invite debate ('Can't you move that?'). A warm, short no is respectful and clear.

steps.prompt: Order these steps for handling someone who keeps pushing after you said no.
steps.hint: Start gentle and get firmer only if they keep pushing.
items: Say no clearly and kindly
If pushed, calmly repeat the same no
Name the pattern: 'I've said no a few times now'
End the conversation or leave if it continues
steps.explain: Start gentle, stay consistent, name the pressure if needed, and remove yourself if they won't respect it. If you ever feel unsafe, leave and get help.

steps.prompt: Which are healthy boundaries? Select all that apply.
options: 'I don't share my passwords, even with close friends.'
'You're not allowed to hang out with anyone but me.'
'I need an hour after work before I talk about stressful stuff.'
'If you yell at me, I'm going to leave the room and we can talk later.'
'You have to text me back within 5 minutes or I'll be upset.'
steps.explain: Healthy boundaries describe your own actions. Controlling who someone sees or how fast they reply is about controlling them, which is a red flag in any relationship.

steps.prompt: Where do you need a boundary right now (time, money, phone, a relationship)? Write the exact words you'll use this week.
